macro.text: Futures slide as the AI sell-off deepens: S&P 500 −2.0%, Nasdaq −3.0%, VIX 30.9; Nvidia −5.4%, Dell down despite raising its sales target a third time.
October PCE: headline +0.3% m/m, 3.8% y/y (as expected); core +0.3% m/m (as expected), 3.3% y/y vs 3.2% expected; income +0.7%, real spending flat. Keeps the Dec 9 hike in place.
Bonds rally on growth fears: 2-year 4.60% (~−7 bp), 10-year 4.85% (~−5 bp), 30-year 5.26%; Dec hike ~98% priced. Gold −1.4% to 3,541, dollar index 103.99.
U.S. proposes new Section 301 tariffs on 14 trading partners incl. China, the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan over overcapacity; country-specific rates after a comment period.
Trump says it is 'probably not too late' for the U.S. to take a stake in Nvidia, though he has not raised it with the company.
Oil steady: WTI 82.51 (+0.6%), Brent 89.27 (+0.6%); OPEC+ meets Nov 29.

sentiment.read: Fear (27), from 11 Friday and 28 Monday, and the number lags the tape: VIX is 30.9 this morning. Good AI news keeps getting sold: Dell's blowout beat and raise went from +3% after hours to −5.9%, Workday beat and raised its year and is −4.9%. sentiment.surprise: Chips holding their opening drop would catch the crowd that sells every good AI headline: NVDA holding 146.20 and reclaiming 150.50, DELL reclaiming 290.50. The other side: a hot core PCE (0.4%+) lifting the 2-year back toward 4.70% would hit the staples that got the money.

Dell's record $132.3B AI backlog and $202B guide were worth +3% after hours and are now −5.9%: orders were in the price; margins are being priced.
VIX 30.9 (+17%), the fear curve above 1.00 and Nasdaq futures −3%: protection is already being paid for.

notPriced.why: Core PCE rose to 3.3% a year (3.2% expected) while real spending was flat: firmer prices with a softer consumer, which bonds were just starting to price away from.

briefs.read: The brief expected a chip-led risk-off day; that held for an hour, then flipped. SPY opened −2.2%, bottomed 695.47 at 9:45, turned up around midday and closed 716.76 (−0.28%, +1.93% from the open; high 2:30). Chip puts sides ran first (NVDA, MU) and failed after 1 p.m.; WDAY, DE and DELL went the calls way. Money left tech for equal-weight and cyclicals. Thursday closed; Friday ends 1 p.m.

readings.name: Fear curve (VIX vs 3-month VIX)
readings.note: above 1.00: traders pay more for protection now than later

sentiment.past: The last five years had this mood on 49 days in 10 separate stretches: the S&P 500 fund was higher five days later 73% of the time (middle result +1.6% after five days, +2.4% after ten).
sentiment.usual: On an ordinary day it was higher five days later 57% of the time.
sentiment.read: The number fell to 21 (Extreme fear) from 27 at Tuesday's close, mostly because junk bonds lagged Treasuries (−2.3% over 10 days) and the fear curve rose to 1.08, but the tape said the opposite by the afternoon. Bad news stopped working: a hot core PCE (3.3% a year), new tariff plans and Nvidia down as much as 9% took SPY to −3.2% by 9:45, and it closed −0.3% (+1.9% from the open). Good and mixed news got bought for the first time this week: Dell filled its whole −9% gap by 2:05 p.m., Deere rose +4.5% on an earnings miss, Workday closed above Tuesday's close. Chips still closed red (NVDA −3.9%, MU −4.1%): sellers finished in the rest of the market first.
sentiment.positioned: Still hedged: VIX closed 28.3 (+7%) even after the rebound, and the fear curve at 1.08 means traders kept paying up for near-term protection into a four-day weekend with a half-day Friday. Money rotated into equal-weight and cyclicals (RSP +0.8%, materials +2.1%, industrials, financials and small caps up) and out of tech (XLK −0.8%, SMH −1.0%). Few are long chips.
sentiment.surprise: A crowd still braced (VIX 28, fear curve above 1.00) would be caught if Friday's thin session extends today's strength: SPY holding above 712.14 (Tuesday's low) with chips joining, NVDA reclaiming 150.50 and MU 609.80. The other side: tariff rates or a weekend headline that sends SPY back under 703.81 (today's opening-range high) would show it was holiday short-covering.
